title: Benefits and trade-offs of multi-vendor operations

opening.headline: Determine the decision criteria between unifying with a single AI vendor or using multiple vendors, balancing selection flexibility against operational complexity.
body: When field opinions differ on whether Service A is better for search and summarization while Service B is better for coding, the organization must decide whether to standardize on a single vendor or to use multiple vendors. Standardizing on one vendor simplifies contracts and security reviews but narrows selection options, whereas using multiple vendors allows choosing strengths for specific needs, but increases the management overhead.

In this class, we first confirm that even with the same model, the entities responsible for authentication, payment, and data processing can differ based on the call path, and that within a single vendor, developer paths and enterprise paths are distinct. Next, we present a table summarizing recurring costs in multi-vendor operations, and follow an explanation that examines an organization where search operations are handled by Company A and coding by Company B, thereby gaining familiarity with the decision-making sequence.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This source explains the benefits and costs associated with multi-vendor operations.
Given the organization's requirements, it is possible to assess whether the vendor configuration is appropriate.

screens.title: Unify into one, or use multiple?
screens.lead: First, let's examine a concern of an organization. As you read, consider what each option offers and what it takes away.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing a unified configuration with a single vendor to a configuration using multiple vendors.

paragraphs: In the field, there's a common opinion that document search and summarization work better with Service A, while code development and review are more effective with Service B. Preferences vary by team, so organizations must decide whether to standardize on a single vendor or use multiple vendors based on specific requirements.

When bundled with a single vendor, contract negotiation, security review, and account management are completed in one go. The responsible party only needs to become familiar with one product. On the other hand, since the vendor must use the same tools in weaker areas, the selection options become limited, and negotiating room decreases when pricing or policies change.

Using multiple vendors allows you to select the right tool for each task and improves negotiation power. However, since certification, authorization, and log formats vary by vendor, conversion and management tasks arise when trying to consolidate the data. The number of management objects effectively multiplies with the number of vendors.
The question to be answered in this class is this: What is the cost of obtaining the right to choose, and in what circumstances is that cost justified?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Just because you use multiple vendors doesn't mean dependency automatically disappears. Check during the class to verify under what conditions dependency remains.

screens.outro: First, let's recall from your experiences what dependency looked like.

screens.title: Recalling the inconvenience of vendor lock-in
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced difficulty switching to an alternative due to price changes?
items.answer: This situation arises because the cost of migration is high. The contract duration, existing workflows, and employees' habits all prevent migration. Negotiating power only emerges as a viable alternative when actual migration is possible, making portability a prerequisite for price negotiations.

items.prompt: Has it ever been difficult to modify a workflow designed specifically for a service's dedicated features?
items.answer: While dedicated features are convenient, they may not be available in other services. Automations and documents built around these features must be recreated when the service changes. This is a typical dependency that arises within a single vendor's ecosystem.

items.prompt: Have you ever had to realign documentation and settings whenever the product name or menu changed?
items.answer: When the product is rebranded, its name and menu structure change, causing existing documentation and configurations to become misaligned with the new names. For example, Vertex AI has been rebranded as the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and a separate official document lists the mapping between the previous and new names. We will revisit this alignment effort in terms of operational costs later.

screens.outro: Now that we've recalled the appearance of dependency, let's examine how the same model varies depending on the path.

screens.title: Same model, different path: The real face of portability
screens.lead: Select each tab to observe the differences among the three ways of calling the Claude model. Compare all three paths at a glance in the last tab.

visual.alt: Diagram showing three call paths converging on a single model and the varying operational entities associated with each path.

tabs.label: Amazon Bedrock
tabs.body:
Claude in Amazon Bedrock operates on infrastructure managed by AWS. The documentation explains that the architecture prevents Anthropic employees from accessing the inference infrastructure and recommends this setup for sensitive applications that require complete execution within AWS. The request format follows forms such as the Messages API.

Authentication supports three paths, with the Bedrock service role being recommended. This approach involves AWS administrators preparing the service role and granting developers the permission to assume that role. In this path, AWS IAM serves as the central authority for access control.

tabs.label: Google Cloud
tabs.body:
The Claude API invoked within Google Cloud's Agent Platform is nearly identical to the Messages API, with two differences in request format. First, the model is specified in the Google Cloud endpoint URL rather than in the request body. Second, anthropic_version is included in the request body rather than in the header, and its value is set to vertex-2023-10-16.

Although these differences appear minor, they mean that code previously used in a different path will fail to work if copied directly. Even when model names are identical, the code used to construct the request and the authentication method must be adjusted to match the specific path.

tabs.label: Claude Platform on AWS
tabs.body:
The Claude Platform on AWS is operated by Anthropic. This distinguishes it from AWS's Bedrock, which operates the inference stack. The documentation describes this as a commercial integration where payments and access are handled through AWS, and specifies that Anthropic is responsible for data processing of inference inputs and outputs.

Authentication is performed using AWS SigV4 signatures or API keys, and AWS handles IAM, marketplace payments, and identity and payment metadata processing. Even if users start with the same AWS account, the entity responsible for data processing differs from Bedrock, necessitating separate reviews of the data processing entity.

tabs.label: comparison summary
tabs.body:
These three paths use the same model series but differ in the items being verified. These include who operates the infrastructure, where the model fits within the request flow, what method is used for authentication, which party handles payment, and who processes the data.

Therefore, portability is not guaranteed simply by having the same model name. When the path changes, the code, authentication mechanisms, and contract reviews must all be updated. When planning for portability, it should be viewed not as merely changing one line of code, but as a comprehensive review of all five of these items.

screens.outro: We will continue with an example where paths branch into two within a single vendor.

screens.title: Two divergent paths even within the same vendor
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the developer pathway and the enterprise pathway differ in Gemini. Also pay attention to the design that makes transitioning between the two paths easy.

states.label: Gemini Developer API
states.body:
The Gemini documentation introduces the Developer API as the fastest path for building, operating, and scaling Gemini-based applications. It advises most developers that they can use this path unless special enterprise-level controls are required.

The code is also simple: just create a client and pass in the model name and input. This approach is well-suited for teams that want to quickly get started and perform lightweight validation. However, when organizational-level identity, network, and data controls become important, teams are encouraged to consider alternative paths.

states.label: Gemini Enterprise Platform
states.body:
The enterprise platform provides business-grade features and services based on Google Cloud. It encompasses everything from model access to agent deployment and management, mentioning more than 200 foundation model access points. As seen in the previously discussed name-change document, Vertex AI services have been consolidated under this platform name.

Both paths can now be accessed through the unified Google GenAI SDK, making transitions easier. When using the enterprise path, the difference lies in specifying the enterprise option, project, and location when creating a client. The structure—same SDK, same invocation pattern, with only the path selection added—demonstrates a well-designed, highly portable architecture.

data.notes: Reusability increases when the design unifies or centralizes the SDK or call points. Methods for reducing overhead costs typically emerge from such designs. The right column of the table does not mean that costs equate to losses; rather, it means that costs are incurred in exchange for gains. The cost should only be borne where the actual gains are needed. The weight of each cost item varies depending on contract size and organizational scale, so it is best to start by estimating the largest items within our organization.

screens.outro: Having verified both costs and compensation, let's now apply this to actual organizational scenarios.

screens.title: Analysis: The organization is divided, with search responsibilities assigned to Company A and coding responsibilities to Company B.
screens.lead: The instructor walks through the process of inspecting an organization that uses two vendors together. Selecting the right arrow proceeds to the next step. Pay attention to what information is gathered before making a judgment.

visual.alt: This is a diagram illustrating the inspection sequence of an organization that uses A company's app and B company's service, presented in five steps.

steps.title: Step 1: Understand the current situation
steps.body: This organization uses A company's app for knowledge search and B company's service for development support. First, we gather facts. We record on one sheet when each service's contract ends, whether separate security reviews were conducted for each, and which department uses which service. At this stage, we do not decide which side is better. The decision is made only after costs and dependencies are clearly identified.

steps.title: Step 2: Compare the authentication.
steps.body: Both services can integrate single sign-on (SSO) authentication. The issue comes next: because their account provisioning methods and authorization models differ, separate actions are required to manage accounts when employees leave or move departments. When account cleanup becomes duplicated, the risk of omission doubles. This cost corresponds to the authentication and authorization items in the table.

steps.title: Step 3: Compare the logs
steps.body: The format of usage records can differ. To report on organizational status, conversion between these two formats is required. If it is not clearly defined who creates and maintains the conversion, reports may reflect only one service. The conversion process must be created once and then continuously maintained, as it needs to be updated each time the service changes.

steps.title: Step 4: Verify the dependency point
steps.body: Now we assess which side depends on dedicated features and which has alternative paths. For example, if a large number of search workflows in the A company's app are built around dedicated features, this indicates a high level of dependency on A company. Conversely, if B company's services are wrapped within a single call point, replacement becomes easier. By listing dependency points, we can estimate future transition costs.

steps.title: Step 5: Compare benefits and costs to make a decision.
steps.body: Finally, compare the quality benefits provided by the two vendors against additional operational costs. If the benefits are certain, retain them with conditions. For example, standardize account provisioning based on the IdP, collect logs in a common format, and review dependency lists on a biweekly basis. If the benefits are unclear, consider an integration approach toward one vendor. The conclusion is that conditional maintenance arrangements are often more appropriate than unconditional retention or unconditional integration.

screens.outro: I will conclude by organizing the checklist in a single criterion.

screens.title: A criterion that swaps options with complexity
screens.lead: I will summarize what I have seen so far into one judgment standard.

paragraphs: Multi-vendor is a choice that trades off options against operational complexity. Options manifest as pricing negotiation power, task-specific optimization, and the ability to circumvent failures, while complexity arises from recurring contracts and security reviews, authentication and log translations, handling of name changes, and dispersion of personnel expertise.

Even with the same model, different call paths result in different request formats, authentication methods, payment handling, and data processing entities. Therefore, portability is determined not by the model name, but by how the path, SDK, and authentication are designed. Within a single vendor, there may be separate developer paths and enterprise paths, but the design of a unified SDK facilitates easy movement between these paths, thereby enhancing portability.

The decision is as follows: deploy the second vendor only in areas where the quality benefit they provide exceeds additional operating costs. In areas where the benefit is unclear, integrate the vendors. By pre-defining dependency points, you can predict transition costs, thereby providing a basis for decisions—whether through negotiation or migration.

Finally, remember one more thing: multi-vendor solutions do not eliminate dependencies. Workflows built with expectations of specialized features may still be tied to a specific vendor. Reducing dependencies is not about increasing the number of vendors, but rather about designing with a wrapper around the caller and using a more standardized interface.

In summary, when evaluating vendor configurations, you should sequentially answer three questions. First, does the second vendor offer a genuine quality difference in this area? Second, is that difference worth more than the additional cost incurred through certification, logging, and review cycles? Third, is there an operating system that can be maintained under conditional requirements? An area where all three answers are affirmative is suitable for a multi-vendor approach. If any of the answers are negative, then a unified approach is preferable.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Multi-vendor is an exchange of choice and complexity. Deploy a second vendor only in areas where the benefit exceeds additional operational costs.

checks.q: Attempting to move the same Claude model via Google Cloud gateway invocation. What is the correct understanding?

checks.explain: In Google Cloud's path model, the model is embedded in the endpoint URL rather than in the request body, and authentication, billing, and data processing responsibilities vary per path, making migration simply a matter of replacement.

wrong.1: Model name alone does not guarantee transferability.
wrong.2: The entities responsible for authentication, payment, and data processing vary by path.
wrong.3: The request body structure has changed. For example, model location and anthropic_version handling differ.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Even if the model name is the same, if the path changes, both the code and authentication will change.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Recall what differs across each path.

glossary.def: It is difficult to migrate due to being tied to a specific vendor's proprietary features, contracts, and formats.
This is merely the capability to move the same task to a different path or vendor. It enhances SDK unification and call separation.
Additional costs arising from contract and security reviews, authentication and log integration, name change responses, and specialization dispersion.
The number of settings, authentication methods, and failure paths that need to be managed has increased.

misconceptions.fact: Workflows designed with specific features may be bundled together within a single vendor's ecosystem across various vendors. Dependency lies not in the number of vendors, but in the design itself.

misconceptions.myth: If the same model is used, it can be used identically regardless of where it is called.
misconceptions.fact: Each path has different request formats, authentication methods, payment mechanisms, and data processing entities. For example, in the Google Cloud path, the model is included in the endpoint URL.

misconceptions.myth: Unifying with a single vendor is always simple and better.
misconceptions.fact: When requirements diverge, simplicity can turn into quality loss. It must be evaluated by comparing benefits against additional operational costs.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Multi-vendor is an exchange of choice and complexity.
Interoperability is determined by the path, SDK, and authentication design, and is not guaranteed solely by the model name.
Place only a second vendor in areas where benefit exceeds additional operating costs.
By pre-defining dependency points in a list, you can predict transition costs.
